idiom_name: duck-typed factory classes (no abstract base required)
implementation_notes: Ruby has no compile-time interface, so the abstract factory is any object that responds to the make_* messages; keeping an AbstractFactory base class is optional and mainly documents the contract, while many codebases skip it and rely on duck typing. Each concrete factory is an ordinary class (or module_function bundle) whose methods return the family's products, and tests substitute any object responding to the same messages (or a test double). Procs/lambdas are available when a family boils down to one creator plus configuration, and `define_method`/`method_missing` can generate family methods when the product kinds are data-driven. For framework integration (Rails, Sidekiq), prefer a class method (e.g., self.factory_for(env)) over a global constant so the selection can be swapped per test context.
code_sketch:
module Factories
  class HtmlFactory
    def make_button(label) = "<button>#{label}</button>"
    def make_slider(lo, hi) = %(<input type="range" min="#{lo}" max="#{hi}">)
  end
end

# the family is whatever duck is injected
render_form(Factories::HtmlFactory.new)
pitfalls: The only contract check is NoMethodError at call time; scattering respond_to? guards through clients hides real mismatches instead of surfacing them.

Stateless factory objects may be safely reused, but class-level mutable state is shared across threads in a process (for example, Puma or Sidekiq); pass request state into the constructor or factory methods.
method_missing/define_method family generators remove the ability to grep for creators, making the family surface implicit; keep an explicit interface comment or a small base module.
Returning nil from a factory method instead of raising is a silent wrong-family attack; prefer raising an ArgumentError with a descriptive message when a product cannot be constructed.
